text:
From: Priya Nair (Head of E-commerce)
Date: Mon 12 Jan, 09:14
Subject: Fwd: OMS - everything in one thread

Forwarding the whole thread so the vendor can read it end to end instead of us writing a brief nobody will believe. Everything below is real and in the order it happened. Start at the bottom if you want the history, start here if you want the summary.

The summary: we sell shoes. 42 stores, our own site on Shopify Plus, and we list on Amazon and Flipkart. Every one of those four channels thinks it owns the stock, and none of them is right. In November we oversold 2,140 orders and cancelled them by hand. The same week we had 1,900 orders that went out as two parcels because the picker could not see that the second size was sitting in the Pune store 4 km from the customer.

We want one system that knows where every pair is, decides who ships it, and tells the customer the truth. That is the project. Everything in this thread is detail under that sentence.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Rahul Menon (CTO)
Date: Fri 9 Jan, 18:42
Subject: Re: OMS - what we are NOT changing

Before anyone proposes a platform migration: Shopify Plus stays. It is the storefront, it works, and the theme took six months. SAP Business One stays, because finance will not move in the same year they moved to it.

What is on the table is the middle: the order management and the inventory truth. Today that is Unicommerce plus two Google Sheets plus a WhatsApp group with the store managers. The sheets are the actual system. If the answer is that we keep Unicommerce and put something on top, say so, I am not attached.

Constraints from my side: hosting in AWS Mumbai, because our data has to stay in India and our team already lives in that account. Postgres or MySQL, nothing exotic, my team is four people. No new ERP. Nothing that requires a Windows server in a store. Every store already has a laptop and a thermal printer, and the network in three stores is a 4G dongle, so a store tool has to survive a bad connection and a browser refresh.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Anand Kulkarni (Warehouse and Ops)
Date: Fri 9 Jan, 16:05
Subject: Re: OMS - what actually goes wrong in the warehouse

From the floor, the problems in the order they cost us money:

1. Allocation. An order comes in for two SKUs. Both show available. One is actually in Bhiwandi, the other is in the Indore store. Nobody decides, so Bhiwandi ships what it has and the rest sits until somebody calls me. If the system allocated the whole order to the nearest location that can complete it, most of this goes away.

2. Store fulfilment. Stores can ship, and three of them are good at it. But they find out about an order when I call them. There is no queue, no accept or reject, no printing from the store. Give them a screen with today's orders, a pick list in aisle order, and a label that prints on the machine they already have.

3. Returns. This is the worst one. A return comes back to whichever warehouse the courier feels like. It is opened, and the SKU goes back into stock three to nine days later, sometimes into the wrong bin. During a sale that stock is worth twice what it is worth in February, and we are holding it in a corner for a week.

4. RTO. Cash on delivery returns to origin are 14% of COD orders. Each one is a parcel that travels twice and a pair that is unavailable for 10 days. I want the RTO parcel scanned at receipt and back into sellable stock the same day.

5. Cycle counting. We count once a quarter and the count is wrong by the time it is finished. I would rather count one aisle a day and have the system tell me which aisle is most likely to be wrong.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Meera Shah (Customer Care)
Date: Thu 8 Jan, 11:30
Subject: Re: OMS - what my team asks for every day

Care handles 3,400 tickets a month and 41% of them are the words "where is my order". My agents open four tabs to answer that: Shopify, Unicommerce, the Delhivery site and the Bluedart site. If the courier has not scanned in two days, we guess.

What I need, in order:
  - One screen per order showing every line, where each line is, and the last scan from whichever courier has it.
  - The ability to cancel a single line, not the whole order, before it is picked.
  - The ability to raise a return or an exchange myself and email the label to the customer, without going to the warehouse.
  - A refund that finance does not have to key in a second time.
  - A note on the order that the next agent can see, so the customer does not repeat their story.

And the customers need the same view without calling us: an order page with the truth on it, and a WhatsApp message when something actually changes. Not eleven emails.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Vikram Iyer (Finance)
Date: Thu 8 Jan, 09:58
Subject: Re: OMS - finance and the money side

Three things from finance and I will stay out of the rest.

First, refunds. Today a refund is raised in Shopify, entered in SAP by hand, and reconciled against the Razorpay settlement file by one person over two days. Whatever we build has to push the refund once and write it once. If your system cannot post to SAP Business One, it has to produce a file our SAP partner accepts, and I want to see that file before we sign.

Second, marketplace settlements. Amazon and Flipkart pay us net of their fees, on their own schedule, with their own return adjustments. Nobody in this company can currently tell you the true margin on a Flipkart order. I would like to, but I accept it may be phase two.

Third, budget, since Priya says the vendor will ask. The board approves the capital number in March. We are a 380-crore revenue business, not an Amazon, and I have seen a proposal that quoted us more than our annual IT spend. Come back with a number that a business our size can sign, and if the right answer is two phases with a gate between them, propose that.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Priya Nair (Head of E-commerce)
Date: Wed 7 Jan, 20:11
Subject: Re: OMS - the numbers, since everyone asked

Volumes, last twelve months:

  Orders per day, normal:            2,900
  Orders per day, sale peak:         9,800 (2 October, and we dropped orders that day)
  Orders per day, target for design: 12,000
  Average lines per order:           1.4
  SKUs live:                         11,400 (style plus colour plus size)
  Stores:                            42, of which 18 can pick and pack today
  Warehouses:                        2 (Bhiwandi and Bangalore), a third opening in Kolkata
  Return rate, own site:             22%
  Return rate, marketplaces:         31%
  COD share of orders:               38%
  RTO rate on COD:                   14%
  Oversell cancellations, November:  2,140
  Split shipments, November:         1,900

The 12,000 number is what we design for, because next Diwali will be bigger and I do not want to have this conversation twice.

From: Rahul Menon (CTO)
Date: Wed 7 Jan, 15:26
Subject: Re: OMS - integrations, and which of them are hard

The ones that must exist on day one:

  Shopify Plus - orders in, fulfilment and tracking back, inventory levels per location. Webhooks, not polling.
  Amazon Seller Central and Flipkart Seller Hub - orders in, dispatch confirmation out, stock out. Both have rate limits that have bitten us.
  Delhivery and Bluedart - manifest, label, pickup request, tracking webhooks. Ekart via Flipkart for their orders.
  Razorpay - the payment record for our own site, refunds, and the settlement file for Vikram.
  SAP Business One - sales invoice, credit note, stock movement. Through our partner's middleware if that is easier.
  WhatsApp Business API - the customer notifications. We already have a provider and a template approval process.
  Unicommerce - only if we keep it. If we replace it, we need its historical orders imported, two years of them.

The ones that are nice to have: Google Sheets export for the merchandising team, who will not give up their sheets and should not have to; and a Slack alert when a channel stops syncing.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Anand Kulkarni (Warehouse and Ops)
Date: Tue 6 Jan, 17:44
Subject: Re: OMS - allocation rules, as we would write them

This is the logic we follow in our heads. It should be a rule table, editable by me, not code a vendor changes.

  Prefer a single location that can ship the complete order.
  Among those, prefer the one nearest the pin code.
  Among those, prefer the warehouse over the store, unless the store has held the item more than 45 days.
  Never allocate to a store on its stock-count day, or on a Sunday in Gujarat.
  Never allocate a COD order to a store, because stores cannot handle the RTO paperwork.
  For a marketplace order, allocate only to a warehouse, because their SLAs are unforgiving.
  If no single location can complete it, split across at most two, and tell the customer honestly that it is coming in two parcels.
  If the item is a pre-order, hold the whole order until the drop date, and say so on the order page.
  A store may reject an order within 30 minutes with a reason; it then reallocates automatically and the rejection is recorded against that store.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Meera Shah (Customer Care)
Date: Tue 6 Jan, 10:02
Subject: Re: OMS - the returns flow, written as the customer sees it

The customer opens their order page and taps return on one line. They pick a reason from a short list and say whether they want a refund, a different size, or a different colour. If it is an exchange, the new pair is reserved at that moment, not when the old one comes back, otherwise the size is gone by Thursday.

We send a label by WhatsApp and by email. The courier picks up from the address on the order unless they change it. The customer sees the pickup scheduled, the pickup done, and the refund state on the same page.

Refund rules that I want enforced by the system and not by my agents: prepaid refunds go back to the original payment method within 48 hours of the quality check passing; COD refunds go to a bank account the customer enters once and we never ask for again; an exchange never waits for a refund; and if the quality check fails, the pair goes back to the customer with a photograph of why, and my team sees that photograph before the customer calls.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Priya Nair (Head of E-commerce)
Date: Mon 5 Jan, 19:50
Subject: Re: OMS - store staff, because we keep forgetting them

Every proposal we have seen treats a store as a warehouse with worse wifi. Our store staff sell shoes; picking is the fourth thing they do in a day. So:

  A store screen with three tabs: to pick, to pack, handed over. Nothing else.
  Pick list sorted the way the stockroom is arranged, which differs by store, so the order is configurable per store.
  Scan the barcode to confirm the pair, because the wrong size goes out otherwise. Every store has a USB scanner.
  One button to print the label on the thermal printer that is already there.
  A daily handover list for the courier with one signature, not one per parcel.
  Click and collect: reserve, notify the customer, hold for 5 days, release automatically with a WhatsApp to the customer saying so.
  If the store laptop loses connection mid-pick, it must not lose the pick. They will not start again.
  Store staff see only their own store, and a regional manager sees their region.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Rahul Menon (CTO)
Date: Mon 5 Jan, 12:18
Subject: Re: OMS - non-functional, since this is where projects die

  Peak: 12,000 orders a day, arriving in two spikes around the sale start times, so roughly 40 orders a minute sustained for an hour.
  Inventory sync: a stock change anywhere is reflected in every channel within two minutes. Today it is 45 minutes and that is the oversell.
  Availability: 99.5% monthly, and the storefront must degrade gracefully rather than block checkout if the OMS is down.
  A store screen has to work on a 4G dongle and a five-year-old laptop.
  No card data touches us, ever. Razorpay holds it and we hold a token.
  Customer personal data stays in India. Logs too.
  Audit: who changed an allocation, who cancelled a line, who edited a rule, kept for three years.
  Roles: store staff, store manager, regional manager, warehouse, care, finance, admin. Care cannot edit a rule and warehouse cannot issue a refund.
  We want the data in our own warehouse (BigQuery today) nightly, so the merchandising team can ask questions without asking you.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Priya Nair (Head of E-commerce)
Date: Mon 5 Jan, 08:30
Subject: Re: OMS - dates and what done means

Dates, and these are not negotiable in the way dates usually are not negotiable:

  Kick-off in the last week of March, after the board meeting.
  Pilot with 3 stores and one warehouse, running real orders, by 15 July.
  All 42 stores and both warehouses live before 20 September. The festive sale starts then and nothing changes after that date, not even a colour.
  Kolkata warehouse onboarded in January next year, by our team, using whatever you have documented.

Done, twelve weeks after full go-live, means:
  Split shipments down 30% against November.
  Oversell cancellations below 1% of orders, from 2.4% today.
  Where-is-my-order tickets down 40%.
  Returned stock sellable again within 24 hours of arriving, against three to nine days.
  Store pick acceptance above 85% within 30 minutes.

If your proposal cannot be measured against those five lines, we will not be able to tell whether it worked, and neither will you.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

From: Sanjay Deshpande (Retail Operations)
Date: Sun 11 Jan, 21:07
Subject: Re: OMS - adding what retail needs, sorry I missed the meeting

Read the whole thread on the train. Two things retail needs that nobody has written down.

One: the store's own stock has to stay sellable in the store. If a customer is standing at the counter with a pair in their hand, no system anywhere may have promised it to someone on the internet in the last four minutes. Whatever the allocation does, the counter wins. Our staff will stop using any tool that makes them apologise to a customer who is physically holding the shoe.

Two: the numbers have to be fair to the store. If a store picks and packs an online order, the sale counts towards that store's target. This sounds like an accounting detail and it is the entire reason 24 of our stores do not fulfil today. Whoever builds this should know that the incentive question decides whether the feature is used.

Also, please do not call it an omnichannel transformation in front of the store managers. Call it the order screen. They will use the order screen.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

MEETING NOTES - internal, 2 January, 11:00 to 13:20
Present: Priya, Rahul, Anand, Meera, Vikram. Apologies: Sanjay (retail ops).

Rahul opened by saying that the November peak was survived by people and not by systems: 14 people in a WhatsApp group reallocating orders by hand for nine days. Nobody disagreed.

Priya walked through the customer complaints from the peak. The pattern was not late delivery, which customers forgive, but wrong information: an order marked shipped that had not been picked, a tracking link that went nowhere for four days, and a cancellation email for an item that was in stock in a store in the same city.

Anand said that the warehouse will accept any system that gives it one queue. His condition is that the allocation rules are his to change, on a screen, without raising a ticket. He has been overruled on this twice before by software that knew better.

Meera asked for the single order view again. She has asked for it in every quarterly review for two years. Agreed that it is the first thing built, before any warehouse feature, because it is what stops the phone ringing.

Vikram asked whether we are buying or building. Rahul's answer: buy the order management, build nothing that a vendor already sells, and keep our four engineers on the storefront and the integrations we cannot outsource.

Discussion on marketplaces. Flipkart is 22% of volume and the hardest SLA. Priya's view is that marketplace orders should never be allocated to a store, and Anand agreed. Vikram noted that marketplace margin is invisible today and asked that the data at least be captured now even if the reporting comes later.

Discussion on the budget. Vikram will take a range to the board in March. He asked the team not to let a vendor design a system that assumes an unlimited number, and asked for a phase one that is useful on its own if phase two never happens.

Actions:
  Priya to write the brief as a forwarded thread rather than a document. Done - this thread.
  Rahul to confirm the integration list with the Shopify and SAP partners. Done, see his message of 7 January.
  Anand to write the allocation rules as he would enforce them. Done, see 6 January.
  Meera to write the returns flow from the customer's side. Done, see 6 January.
  Vikram to get a settlement file sample from Razorpay for the vendor. Pending.
